“These thoughts soothed me, and in the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep. But the fever in my blood would not allow peaceful dreams. The terrible scene of the day before kept playing before my eyes: the women fleeing, and Felix, furious, dragging me away from his father's feet. I woke exhausted. Discovering that night had already come, I crept out of my hiding place to look for food.

“When I had eaten enough, I followed the familiar path towards the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I slipped into my shelter and waited silently for the usual hour when the family got up. That hour came and went, and the sun rose high in the sky, but none of them appeared. I began trembling violently, afraid that some terrible misfortune had happened. The cottage was dark inside, and I heard no movement. I cannot describe the suffering of that uncertain wait.

“After a while, two countrymen passed. They stopped near the cottage and began talking, waving their arms forcefully. I could not understand them because they spoke the local language, which was different from the language my protectors used. Soon afterwards, however, Felix arrived with another man. This surprised me, since I knew he had not left the cottage that morning. I waited anxiously, hoping their conversation would explain these strange events.

“‘Have you considered,’ his companion asked, ‘that you will have to pay three months' rent and give up everything growing in your garden? I don't want to take unfair advantage of you. Please take a few days to think over your decision.’

“‘That would be completely useless,’ Felix answered. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father's life is in very great danger because of the dreadful event I have described. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. I beg you not to argue with me any longer. Take back your property and let me escape from this place.’

“Felix shook violently as he spoke. He and the other man went into the cottage, stayed a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

“For the rest of that day, I remained in my shelter, numb with absolute despair. My protectors had gone, breaking the only bond that connected me to the world. For the first time, my heart filled with hatred and a desire for revenge. I made no effort to resist those feelings. Instead, I let them carry me along like a current and turned my thoughts towards causing suffering and death.

“No, no, that is to-morrow; and it was precisely on that account that I particularly wished to see Knightley to-day. Such a frightfully scorching morning! And I came across the fields”—his voice suggested great ill-treatment—“which made everything worse. Then to discover him away from home! I assure you, I am far from pleased. No apology, no message left for me. The housekeeper insisted she knew nothing of my being expected. Most extraordinary! And not a soul could tell me where he had gone. Perhaps Hartfield, perhaps the Abbey Mill, perhaps his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley! Can you account for it?”

Emma entertained herself by declaring that it was extraordinary indeed and that she could not offer a word in his defence.

“I cannot conceive,” said Mrs. Elton, feeling the affront as a wife properly should, “I cannot conceive how he could treat you so, of all people! The very last person one would think he could forget! My dear Mr. E., surely he left you a message; I am certain he did. Even Knightley cannot be quite so eccentric. His servants must have forgotten it. Depend on that being the explanation, and it is just what one might expect of the Donwell servants, who, as I have frequently noticed, are exceedingly clumsy and neglectful. Nothing would induce me to have such a creature as his Harry waiting at our sideboard. And Wright thinks very little indeed of Mrs. Hodges. She promised Wright a receipt and never forwarded it.”

“I encountered William Larkins,” Mr. Elton continued, “as I approached the house. He told me his master was out, but I would not believe him. William appeared rather cross. He said he could not tell what had come over his master lately; he could scarcely ever secure a word with him. William's requirements are no concern of mine, but it really is most important that I see Knightley to-day. Consequently, having undertaken this hot walk for nothing is a very serious inconvenience.”

Emma thought her wisest course was to return home at once. Very probably she was being waited for there at that moment; and Mr. Knightley might thus be saved from committing further offences against Mr. Elton, if not against William Larkins.

On taking leave, she was glad to find Miss Fairfax intent upon seeing her out of the room and accompanying her even down the stairs. This afforded an opportunity of which she immediately availed herself, to say,

One might have thought, looking at him, that Nemesis had taken the shield of Pallas and confronted him with the Gorgon's head. He appeared petrified, his sorrowful face as still as marble. Until now he had enjoyed the refined, luxurious existence of a well-born and wealthy young man, a life made exquisite by its freedom from sordid anxieties and its lovely, boyish carelessness. For the first time he now understood the dreadful mystery of Destiny and the terrible significance of Doom.

How monstrous and insane it seemed! Was some fearful secret of sin inscribed upon his hand, some crimson token of crime, in characters unreadable to him but intelligible to another? Could there truly be no escape? Were we merely pieces upon a chessboard moved by an invisible hand, vessels shaped at a potter's pleasure for honour or disgrace? His reason rebelled; nevertheless, he felt a tragedy suspended above him and knew that he had suddenly been summoned to carry an unbearable weight. How fortunate actors are! They may decide whether to play in comedy or tragedy, to rejoice or suffer, to laugh or weep. Actual life allows no such choice. Most women and men must undertake roles for which they are unsuited. Our Guildensterns are required to act Hamlet, while our Hamlets must make jokes like Prince Hal. The world may be a stage, but its casting is wretched.

At that moment Mr. Podgers came into the room. He started at the sight of Lord Arthur, and his heavy, coarse face assumed a greenish-yellow tint. Their eyes met, and neither spoke for an instant.

“The Duchess has forgotten a glove here, Lord Arthur, and requested that I fetch it,” Mr. Podgers said at last. “Ah, there it is upon the sofa! Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I must require a plain answer to a question I intend to ask you.”

“Some other time, Lord Arthur; the Duchess is waiting anxiously. I fear I must leave.”

“You shall do no such thing. The Duchess is not in haste.”

“One should never keep ladies waiting, Lord Arthur,” said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. “The fair sex tends to impatience.”

Lord Arthur's delicately modelled lips curved with fretful contempt. At that moment the unfortunate Duchess seemed utterly insignificant to him. He crossed to Mr. Podgers and extended his hand.

“Tell me what you read there,” he said. “Give me the truth. I must know. I am no child.”
